blocks.prompt: The Squishy Machine Inside Your Head
blocks.text: Your brain sits inside your skull. The skull is a hard bone helmet. It keeps your brain safe. Your brain is about the size of two fists put together. It is soft, like thick jelly. Your brain sends tiny messages all through your body. The messages travel fast, faster than a race car. When you want to wiggle your toes, your brain sends the message down and your toes wiggle right away. Your brain does not take a break. It works while you sleep. It sorts out what you did today so you can remember it tomorrow.

blocks.prompt: The Machine That Never Turns Off
blocks.text: Your brain weighs about three pounds. That is about as heavy as a small loaf of bread. It does not look like much. It is grayish, wrinkled, and soft enough to dent with a finger. But that squishy lump is doing every single thing you call being you. Your brain is packed with tiny cells called neurons. You have about eighty six billion of them. Neurons talk to each other using tiny sparks of electricity. A thought is a pattern of those sparks, racing from neuron to neuron. The wrinkles matter. If you could pull your brain flat like a sheet, it would be much bigger than your head. Folding it up is how all that surface fits inside your skull. Here is the strangest part. Your brain has no pain sensors of its own. It tells you when your knee hurts, but it cannot feel itself. Surgeons can operate on a brain while the person is awake and talking.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Two percent of your weight, twenty percent of your energy
It runs on about 20 watts, like a dim bulb
Neurons pass messages across gaps called synapses
Myelin insulates a nerve fiber like a wire
Signals can move at over 200 miles per hour

blocks.prompt: Twenty Watts of You
blocks.text: Your brain makes up about two percent of your body weight. It burns about twenty percent of your energy. Every breakfast you eat, one fifth of it goes straight to the three pound organ sitting quietly in your skull, doing nothing you can see. What is it spending all that on? Signals. Your brain holds roughly eighty six billion neurons, and each one may connect to thousands of others. When a neuron fires, a pulse of electricity runs down a long fiber called an axon. At the end, the pulse turns into a chemical message that jumps a microscopic gap to the next cell. That gap is a synapse. Everything you have ever remembered, feared, or figured out happened as traffic across those gaps. Some axons are wrapped in a fatty sleeve called myelin. Myelin works like the insulation on a wire, and it makes signals travel far faster. An unwrapped fiber creeps along. A wrapped one can carry a signal at over two hundred miles per hour. Your brain also rebuilds itself. Learning is not the brain filling up like a bucket. It is the brain physically changing: strengthening the connections you use, and quietly letting go of the ones you do not. Scientists call this plasticity. It is why a skill you practice every day gets easier, and why one you abandon slips away.

notes: The hippocampus is named for its seahorse shape

blocks.prompt: What Henry Forgot
blocks.text: In 1953, a young man named Henry Molaison lay on an operating table in Hartford, Connecticut. He had suffered violent seizures for years and nothing had stopped them. A surgeon removed a small structure from deep inside each side of his brain, a seahorse shaped piece called the hippocampus. The seizures eased. Something else broke. Henry woke up unable to form new memories. Not damaged memories. No new ones at all. He could hold a conversation, work a puzzle, and crack a joke, because his short term memory was intact. But the moment his attention moved on, the last few minutes were gone completely. He met the same researcher thousands of times across fifty years and greeted her as a stranger every time. He read the same magazine with fresh interest. He was, in his own words, like someone always waking from a dream. Henry became the most studied patient in the history of neuroscience, and he taught us something nobody had suspected: memory is not one thing. It is several separate systems living in different parts of the brain. Here is the proof. Researchers asked Henry to trace a star while looking only at its reflection in a mirror, which is far harder than it sounds. Every session, he insisted he had never attempted the task before. Every session, he did it better than the last. His hands were learning while his conscious mind recorded nothing. Skill memory and event memory run on different machinery, and his surgery had removed only one of them. Henry could also remember his childhood clearly. That mattered too. It meant the hippocampus is not the warehouse where old memories are stored. It is the loading dock, the place where new experiences are processed and passed along to the rest of the brain for keeping. Take away the dock and the warehouse survives, but nothing new gets in. Henry Molaison died in 2008 at eighty two. He had agreed, decades earlier, to donate his brain. It was frozen, sliced into two thousand four hundred and one wafer thin sections, and photographed. Anyone can look at them online. He never knew he was famous. He could not have held on to the fact for more than a minute.

6.title: The Squishy Machine Inside Your Head
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Squishy Machine Inside Your Head

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: A newborn has most of the neurons it will ever have
Synaptic pruning removes the connections you do not use
Myelination runs back to front, finishing in the mid twenties
The prefrontal cortex matures last
London cab drivers memorize about 25,000 streets
The ten percent myth is false
The brain runs on roughly 20 watts

blocks.prompt: The Brain That Deletes Itself
blocks.text: Your brain is not built the way a house is built, by adding rooms until it is finished. It is built the way a sculptor works, by starting with too much and taking away. A newborn arrives with most of the neurons it will ever have. What it does not have is wiring. Over the first two years, those neurons throw out connections at a furious rate, forming synapses far faster than experience could ever justify. By age two or three, parts of a child's cortex carry many more synaptic connections than an adult brain does. The child is over-built on purpose. It is a guess about every possible world it might have been born into. Then the brain starts cutting. Connections that carry traffic get reinforced. Connections that sit idle are dismantled and their materials recycled. Neuroscientists call this synaptic pruning, and it is not damage. It is the main event. A brain that kept every connection would be slow, noisy, and unable to decide anything. Sculpting is how a general purpose organ becomes your specific mind, shaped by the language you actually heard and the hands you actually used. This is also why early experience carries weight that later experience does not. A newborn can hear every sound distinction used by every human language on Earth. By about a year old, that ability has narrowed to the sounds that showed up around it. The unused discriminations were not forgotten. They were pruned. Pruning does not stop in childhood. It runs a second campaign through adolescence, and this time it concentrates on the prefrontal cortex, the region behind your forehead responsible for planning, weighing consequences, and interrupting an impulse before it becomes an action. At the same time, axons across the brain are being wrapped in myelin, the fatty insulation that speeds a signal up. Myelination sweeps roughly from the back of the brain toward the front, and the prefrontal cortex is last in line. It is not finished until the mid twenties. That timeline explains a great deal. The brain's reward and emotion systems come online early, in the first years of the teens. The prefrontal system that regulates them arrives late. For roughly a decade, an adolescent is driving a car whose engine matured before its brakes did. This is not a character flaw, and it is not a story about bad teenagers. It is a construction schedule. The upside of an unfinished brain is that an unfinished brain learns. Consider London taxi drivers, who must memorize roughly twenty five thousand streets to earn a license. Researchers scanned them and found the rear portion of their hippocampus, a memory structure, was measurably enlarged compared to other drivers, and that it was larger the longer they had been on the job. Their brains had physically restructured around a demand placed on them. That capacity is called plasticity, and it is worth being precise about, because it gets abused. You may have heard that people only use ten percent of their brains. That claim is false and always has been. Scans show activity distributed across the entire organ, and there is no silent ninety percent waiting to be switched on. Evolution does not maintain an organ that burns a fifth of your daily energy so that most of it can idle. The real finding is more interesting than the myth. You do use all of your brain. What changes is the wiring, continuously, in response to what you do. Every skill you practice thickens a path. Every one you drop gets quietly reclaimed. The brain you have at thirty is, in a literal physical sense, a record of what you spent your time on.
